segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when he opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I saw the seven angels who stand before God, and seven trumpets were given to them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And another angel came and stood at the altar, holding a golden censer, and much incense was given to him to offer with the prayers of all the holy ones on the golden altar that is before the throne.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the smoke of the incense went up with the prayers of the holy ones from the angel’s hand before God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the angel took the censer and filled it with fire from the altar and threw it to the earth, and there came peals of thunder and rumblings and flashes of lightning and an earthquake.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the seven angels who had the seven trumpets prepared themselves to sound them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The first sounded his trumpet, and there came hail and fire mixed with blood, and it was thrown to the earth; and a third of the earth was burned up, and a third of the trees were burned up, and all the green grass was burned up.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The second angel sounded his trumpet, and something like a great mountain burning with fire was thrown into the sea; and a third of the sea became blood,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and a third of the creatures in the sea, those that had life, died, and a third of the ships were destroyed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The third angel sounded his trumpet, and a great star fell from the sky, burning like a torch, and it fell on a third of the rivers and on the springs of water.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The name of the star is Wormwood. And a third of the waters became wormwood, and many people died from the waters, because they had been made bitter.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The fourth angel sounded his trumpet, and a third of the sun was struck, and a third of the moon, and a third of the stars, so that a third of them would be darkened, and the day would not shine for a third of it, and the night likewise.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I looked, and I heard an eagle flying high overhead, saying with a loud voice,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth, because of the remaining trumpet blasts of the three angels who are about to sound!”

notes.note: The Greek gives no subject. The one opening the seals is the Lamb, who began opening them in chapter 6; some translations supply “the Lamb” here for clarity.

The text does not explain the silence, and interpreters differ. Some take it as the hush of awe before God acts in judgment, a motif found in the prophets; others connect it with the incense offering that follows, as though heaven falls quiet so that the prayers of God's people may be heard.

notes.phrase: the seven angels who stand before God
notes.note: The definite article points to a group the readers were expected to know. Jewish tradition spoke of seven angels who attend in God's immediate presence (for example Tobit 12:15), later often called archangels.

The traditional rendering is “saints,” which now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The Greek term is used of all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God's people.”

The Greek is a bare dative, here and in verse 4. It may mean the incense is offered together with the prayers, or on behalf of the prayers, or even that the incense represents the prayers themselves (compare 5:8). “With” is the most common rendering and leaves the relationship open.

The Greek word means both “voice” and “sound.” Older versions have “voices,” but most modern translations render “rumblings.” The cluster of thunder, sounds, lightning and earthquake recalls God's appearance at Sinai in Exodus 19 and recurs in Revelation at climactic moments.

notes.phrase: hail and fire mixed with blood
notes.note: The trumpet judgments echo the plagues on Egypt in Exodus: hail with fire, water turned to blood, and darkness. A reader steeped in the Scriptures would have recognised the pattern of God judging an oppressor before delivering his people.

The same Greek word means both “heaven” and “sky.” It is rendered “heaven” in verse 1, where God's dwelling is in view, and “sky” here, where a star falls. Some translations keep “heaven” here; the Greek does not distinguish the two.

Wormwood is an intensely bitter plant. In the Hebrew Scriptures it is an image of bitter suffering and divine judgment (for example Jeremiah 9:15), and the name here signals what the star does to the waters. The plant itself is not normally deadly; the image is symbolic.

The earliest and best manuscripts read “eagle”; many later manuscripts read “angel,” which is why the King James Version has “an angel.” The Greek word can also mean a vulture, a bird associated with impending death, and some interpreters prefer that sense here.

The Greek word is an astronomical term for the highest point of the sky, where the sun stands at noon. “Midheaven” or “the midst of heaven” is the traditional rendering, but it can suggest a region halfway up or a middle tier of heaven. The point is that the eagle is at the zenith, visible and audible to all.

candidates.reason: Occurs three times in Revelation (8:13; 14:6; 19:17) and translations vary between midheaven, midair and overhead; it should be rendered identically in all three.
“Those who dwell on the earth” is a recurring near-technical phrase in Revelation for humanity opposed to God, and its wording (dwell/live/inhabitants) should be fixed across the book.
The word covers voice, sound and noise, and the recurring storm formula in Revelation (4:5; 8:5; 11:19; 16:18) needs one consistent rendering.
Rendered variously as soul, life, self or person across the New Testament; no register entry was supplied for its use here of animal life.
Recurs across the Gospels and Revelation; translators vary between “woe,” “alas” and “how terrible,” and the three “woes” of Revelation depend on a fixed rendering.
